headline: Run HPKE over a SHAKE key schedule, and encrypt to a P-384 recipient.
summary: HPKE gains the two single-stage KDFs of the post-quantum HPKE draft, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256. A single-stage KDF has one Derive where HKDF has an extract and an expand, so the key schedule is a different construction: the key, the base nonce and the exporter secret are consecutive slices of one squeeze. Select them with `pki.hpke.suites.KDF.SHAKE128` or `SHAKE256`; `setupS`, `setupR`, `seal`, `open` and `export` take them unchanged. DHKEM(P-384, HKDF-SHA384) ships alongside, the one RFC 9180 KEM the module did not offer.

Added: The HPKE single-stage KDFs SHAKE128 (0x0010) and SHAKE256 (0x0011), with the one-stage key schedule of draft-ietf-hpke-hpke sec. 5.1 behind them. One LabeledDerive of Nk + Nn + Nh bytes replaces the two-stage schedule's extract-and-expand chain, and `Context.export` derives through LabeledDerive rather than LabeledExpand. Nh is 32 for SHAKE128 and 64 for SHAKE256, taken from the KDF's definition rather than an extract width. Both are verified through the shipped verbs against Appendix A.7, A.8, A.11 and A.12 of draft-ietf-hpke-pq: the key pair derived from each vector's ikm, the published encapsulated key decapsulated under it, then all ten opens and all five exports.

`pki.hpke.suites.KEM.DHKEM_P384_HKDF_SHA384` (0x0011), in all four modes with every KDF and AEAD. Nsecret is 48, the public key and the encapsulated key are 97 bytes, and the private key is a 48-byte scalar; Appendix A.8 of draft-ietf-hpke-pq is its known-answer vector.

`hpke/input-length`, thrown when `opts.info`, `opts.psk` or `opts.pskId` exceeds 65535 bytes on a single-stage KDF. The one-stage schedule prefixes each with a two-byte length (draft-ietf-hpke-hpke sec. 7.2.1 states the bound as a MUST), so a longer input has no encoding; refusing it keeps a sender and a recipient from deriving different keys from inputs each accepted. An export longer than 65535 is refused with `hpke/export-length` for the same reason. A two-stage KDF keeps its own limits and is unaffected.

TurboSHAKE128 (0x0012) and TurboSHAKE256 (0x0013) are registered in the same table and are not offered: no released OpenSSL exposes either extendable-output function, and `node:crypto` on OpenSSL 3.5.8 answers "Digest method not supported" for both. A request for one is refused with `hpke/unknown-suite`. They ship when the runtime carries them.
Fixed: `pki.possession.verifyRequest` accepted a signature certificate whose `keyUsage` does not permit signing. A certificate confined to `keyAgreement` could authorize a certification request, so a key never issued for signing could authorize issuance. RFC 5280 sec. 4.2.1.3 confines a key to the purposes a present keyUsage asserts, and the verdict now reports `signerMaySign` and makes `valid` false when it is false, with the signature's own verdict kept separate. Any of `digitalSignature`, `contentCommitment` or `nonRepudiation` permits it, a certificate carrying no keyUsage is unconfined and still accepted, and a keyUsage that does not decode denies.

Where a verb has a size limit, the limit is now read before its input is copied rather than after. `pki.tlog.parseTile`, `parseEntryBundle` and `parseNote`, and the single-stage `info`, `psk` and `psk_id` of `pki.hpke`, each copy their input so the bytes checked are the bytes used; an oversized input was copied in full and only then refused. A 64 MiB buffer handed to a parser whose tiles are 8192 bytes now allocates nothing. Each keeps the verdict it had: an over-wide tile is still `tlog/bad-tile`.

`pki.tlog.parseNote` checked a note for ASCII control characters but not for valid UTF-8, which C2SP signed-note requires of both. A malformed byte was replaced with U+FFFD instead of refused, so a correctly signed checkpoint beginning with 0xFF verified with its origin reported as U+FFFD and the text reported did not encode back to the bytes signed. The whole note is now decoded strictly before any of it is read, and a note that is not valid UTF-8 is refused with `tlog/bad-note`.

`pki.tlog.parseEntryBundle` bounded an entry bundle by its byte length but not by its entry count. A zero-length entry costs two bytes on the wire and an object in memory, so a megabyte of zero bytes decoded into half a million entries and the permitted 16 MiB input could allocate hundreds of megabytes and block the event loop. The count is capped at 256, one tile's width, which is the bound C2SP tlog-tiles states; `pki.C.LIMITS.TLOG_MAX_ENTRY_BUNDLE_ENTRIES` names it.

`pki.tlog` returned tile hashes and bundle entries as views into the bytes handed to it, and the bytes come from the caller's own `read` callback. A callback that reuses one scratch buffer between tile fetches, which a real one may, had a later fetch overwrite proof nodes already collected, so `pki.tlog.inclusionProof` returned a proof that did not fold to the tree head the log served. Every byte input to the module is copied at the door now.

`pki.tuf.parseMetadata` accepted a fractional or exponent-form number where TUF's canonical JSON admits only integers. A version written `1.0000000000000001` converts to the number 1, so the integer check that followed saw a conforming document and the version reported was not the one the bytes stated. Numbers are now refused while they are still text, with `tuf/bad-json`, which is what the format requires; the shared JSON reader gained an integers-only policy for callers whose format forbids floating point.

The ACME client read the transport's response body and status per use rather than once. The transport is a caller-supplied option, so its response is a caller object: the body whose length was measured against `maxResponseBytes` need not be the body handed back. Both are read once now. This one carries no behavioral vector, because the test transport normalizes the body before the client sees it.

Several verbs read a value out of the caller's own object more than once, or after awaiting, so an object answering each read differently could pass a check with one value and be acted on with another. `pki.acme.verifyTlsAlpn01` validated the identifier's name and then compared a second read of it against the certificate's SAN, so a name nothing validated could be matched and the identifier reported as confirmed. `pki.acme.externalAccountBinding` validated one account JWK and could bind another; `pki.acme.finalize` validated one identifier list and could assert the CSR against another; `pki.acme.keyChange` could sign its inner and outer JWS for different `url` values. `pki.jose.sign` adopted one key for signing and computed the expected signature width from a second read of it. `pki.ct.verifySctWithLogList` reported a timestamp read after verification rather than the one the signature covered, and `pki.ct.fetchLogList` read `requireJsonContentType` only after the request returned. Each of those verbs now reads the members named once, at entry, and runs every check and every result off those values. The same pattern one level deeper, a field inside a record a caller supplies, is not covered by this release.

`pki.ct.addChain` read `opts.chain[0]` twice, once to build the submitted body and once to build the entry the returned SCT is verified over. A caller whose array answered the two reads with different certificates would submit one and have the log's receipt accepted as a receipt for the other. Each element is copied once now and both the request and the check are derived from that copy.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` read `opts.fulcioRoots` and `opts.ctLogs` at the point of use, which is after the timestamp check has already awaited. A caller could pass no anchor, add one while verification was pending, and have the chain accepted against material the call was not made with. Both lists, and the Rekor keys with them, are normalized before the first await.

`pki.ct` held a caller's bytes as a view onto their buffer rather than a copy, and its verbs import a key with an await before they verify. An RSA signed tree head whose signature buffer was overwritten in that window was verified against the replacement rather than against the bytes supplied at entry, so `pki.ct.verifySth` could return true for a signature the caller never passed. Every byte input to the module is now copied at the door, which covers `verifySth`, `verifySct`, `addChain`, the log-list check and the entry builders alike. An ECDSA signature was never exposed, its DER-to-P1363 conversion having copied it already.

`pki.relatedCert.verifyRequest` encoded `certID` twice, once into the signed preimage and once for the comparison against the certificate. A caller whose `certID`, or whose `issuer` or `serialNumber` inside it, answered each read differently could have the proof hashed over one identifier and compared against another, so a proof made for one certificate would verify against a second certificate sharing its public key. The identifier is now encoded once and those bytes are used for both.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` read the pinned Rekor keys from the caller's own objects at each check, and the checkpoint and the signed entry timestamp are verified on either side of an await. A caller that replaced a key record in between could have the two authenticated under different key material filed under one log identifier. The pinned keys are now copied, field by field and window included, before the first await, and each field is read from the caller exactly once.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` took the first RFC 3161 timestamp that verified and refused the bundle if the Fulcio certificate was not valid at that instant. A signature re-timestamped while it is archived carries more than one token, and the one listed first need not be the one made at signing, so a bundle another token dates inside the certificate's life was refused with `sigstore/chain-invalid`. Every verified timestamp is now a candidate and each is tried, as the transparency-log entries already were. The number of combinations tried is bounded by the same per-list cap, and a bundle asking for more is refused.

`pki.hpke.setupS` and `seal` accepted `opts.eph`, a fixed sender ephemeral key pair, on a PQ/T hybrid suite and then generated a random encapsulation instead, so a caller who named a key got a success that did not use it. A hybrid takes its encapsulation randomness from the runtime, as ML-KEM does, and now refuses `opts.eph` with `hpke/bad-input` the way the ML-KEM suites already did. The DHKEM suites honor it unchanged.

`pki.hpke` checked the width of a raw key, seed or encapsulated key by reading its `length`, which a Buffer can carry as an own property that differs from its real byte count. A value longer than the suite's width could therefore pass the check and have its extra bytes used. `decap` accepted a 64-byte encapsulated key reporting 32 and folded the hidden suffix into the KEM context, so changing only those extra bytes changed the shared secret it returned; `encap` accepted a 64-byte DHKEM public key reporting 32; and `decap` accepted a 64-byte hybrid seed reporting 32. Every byte a caller supplies is now snapshotted before any width is read, so the length checked is the length used, and an over-long value is refused with `hpke/bad-key`. This covers `setupS`, `setupR`, `seal`, `open`, `encap`, `decap`, `opts.eph` and `opts.senderKey`, and it also means a caller holding a reference can no longer change those bytes after they are checked.
